name: Central African Republic
summary_text: Private same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal in the Central African Republic for both men and women. Criminal liability attaches only to public conduct.  Article 85 of the criminal code punishes public expression of love between persons of the same sex as an attack on public morals. The penalty is imprisonment of six months to two years or a fine of 150,000 to 600,000 CFA francs. The law treats this conduct more severely than other public moral offences.  Where one participant is a child, the adult faces imprisonment of two to five years or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs.  Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A trans visitor cannot change a gender marker and will be assessed against documents as issued.  No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education, or access to goods and services. A visitor refused care, service, or assistance has no statutory basis for a complaint, according to the United States State Department 2023 report.  Same-sex couples have no legal recognition. Article 7 of the Constitution defines marriage as the union between one man and one woman and bans same-sex marriage. Public affection between same-sex partners falls within reach of the public morals provision.  Alternatives Centrafrique, founded in 2009 and registered in 2020, documented mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement, including arrests based on false accusations of same-sex intercourse. The United States State Department reported that criminalisation of public same-sex activity had pushed the community underground.  Societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was described as entrenched. Many citizens attributed homosexuality to undue outside influence. Other accounts described same-sex conduct as taboo, viewed as imported from outside the region and contrary to local values. The community conceals itself. Maintaining queer relationships was described as dangerous.  No transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody, or care rule was sourced beyond the absence of gender recognition. All other rules affecting a trans visitor are stated on an LGBTQ-collective basis.  Two narrow formal protections were sourced. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data treats sexual orientation as sensitive data, with Article 17 prohibiting any processing of sensitive data due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. The Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement condemning violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Neither creates an enforceable remedy for refusal of service or police abuse.

name: Côte d'Ivoire
summary_text: Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalized.  Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes public breach of decency with three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or contrary-to-nature act with an individual of the same sex, the penalty is six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled if committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor of eighteen years.  Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for homosexual couples and 15 for heterosexual couples.  Côte d'Ivoire provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. No legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation exists either.  The government does not recognize same-sex couples.  The United States Department of State 2023 report on human rights practices records three deaths within the LGBTQI+ community during that year. In the same year a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Police responses to such non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years. Many victims do not report to police because they believe they will not be taken seriously.  In September and October 2024, 45 assault incidents were recorded in Abidjan. Social media influencers called for violence during that period. A homophobia-motivated attack occurred at a market employing gay hair stylists. After these attacks people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant.  Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face an especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaks social norms and draws hostile attention. Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born anatomically male who live as women, face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention.  During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d’Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers. Complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals. Fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis, defined as transgender and otherwise gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth. In 2012 members of the same force repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar in Abidjan frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases.  In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis, gay men and trans women, and lelés, lesbians and trans men, stating that despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to customs and traditions, members of this woubi community remain human beings and benefit from human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties. In 2024 President Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to counter the expansion of homosexuality.  Discrimination in healthcare continues, including refusal of care on grounds of sexual orientation.
